Usually not. They are the fundamental (12 months) and the harmonics of one annual pattern that is not shaped like a sine wave. I would report a single twelve-month cycle and note that the 6- and 4-month peaks are its harmonics, as in the December-spike panel of @fig-harmonics.

### Step 3: do not trust a single tall ordinate

```{r}
#| label: fig-wn_pgram
#| fig-cap: "Raw periodograms of white noise for three sample sizes. The true spectrum is flat at 1 (purple line). The estimates do not settle down as n grows: there are just more of them."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

set.seed(7)
wn_pg = bind_rows(lapply(c(64, 256, 1024), function(n) {
  pgram(rnorm(n)) |> mutate(n = paste0("n = ", n))
}))
wn_pg$n = factor(wn_pg$n, levels = c("n = 64", "n = 256", "n = 1024"))

ggplot(wn_pg, aes(freq, I)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = freq, yend = 0), colour = col_bar, linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = col_ref) +
  facet_wrap(~n, ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = expression(I(f)), title = "White noise periodograms.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

::: callout-note
## The raw periodogram is unbiased but not consistent

Each ordinate estimates $S(f)$ correctly on average, but its standard deviation is about as large as its mean and does not shrink as $n$ grows (@fig-wn_pgram). For white noise each ordinate is approximately $S(f)$ times an exponential random variable.
:::

**Question: one very tall peak in a raw periodogram. Does that prove a real cycle?**

No. There are many ordinates and each one is very noisy, so some will always look large by chance. To separate real cycles from noise I need to smooth the spectrum (Step 4) and test the largest peak (Step 5).

### Step 4: smooth, and keep what survives

Neighbouring ordinates estimate almost the same value of a smooth spectrum, so averaging them reduces the noise. In `spec.pgram()` the `spans` argument sets how many neighbours are averaged.

```{r}
#| label: fig-ar2_smooth
#| fig-cap: "Periodogram of one simulated AR(2) series with no smoothing and with three increasing spans, against the true spectral density (purple), on a log scale."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

set.seed(11)
ar2_phi = c(1.5, -0.75)
y_ar2 = arima.sim(list(ar = ar2_phi), n = 512)

spans_list = list("No smoothing" = NULL, "spans = 5" = 5, "spans = 11" = 11, "spans = 31" = 31)
ar2_sm = bind_rows(lapply(names(spans_list), function(nm) {
  sp = spec.pgram(y_ar2, spans = spans_list[[nm]], taper = 0.1, plot = FALSE)
  tibble(freq = sp$freq, spec = sp$spec, smoothing = nm)
}))
ar2_sm$smoothing = factor(ar2_sm$smoothing, levels = names(spans_list))
ar2_true = tibble(freq = seq(0.001, 0.5, length.out = 500)) |>
  mutate(spec = arma_spec(freq, ar = ar2_phi))

ggplot(ar2_sm, aes(freq, spec)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_bar) +
  geom_line(data = ar2_true, colour = col_ref, linewidth = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~smoothing, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = "Spectral density (log scale)", title = "Smoothing the periodogram.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

**Question: what goes wrong if the span is too small or too large?**

Too small: the estimate stays noisy and real features are hard to see (top left of @fig-ar2_smooth). Too large: neighbouring features are averaged together, so peaks are flattened and troughs filled in (`spans = 31` is lower and wider at the peak than the true density). In practice I compare a few spans and trust the features that survive a moderate increase in smoothing.

### Step 5: test the largest peak

Fisher's test compares the largest ordinate with the sum of all of them, $g = \max_j I(f_j)/\sum_j I(f_j)$, and its null distribution accounts for having picked the maximum.

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
fisher_g_test(rnorm(240))   # white noise: large p-value expected
fisher_g_test(y_cyc)        # the period-24 series: tiny p-value expected
```

**Question: what is the null hypothesis, and what does rejecting it mean?**

The null hypothesis is that the series is white noise. Rejecting it is evidence of periodic structure compared to white noise. It does not prove that a particular (for example deterministic seasonal) model is correct. If the series is autocorrelated, the test can reject just because correlated noise does not have a flat spectrum. In that case the cycle should be tested on the residuals of a fitted ARMA model, and the p-value is then only approximate (see the [topic exploration](#topic-exploration-is-the-lynx-cycle-a-real-cycle) below).

## Preparing a series

The three routine steps are all `spec.pgram()` defaults: remove the mean (and usually the trend), taper the ends, and (cosmetically) pad the series.

```{r}
#| label: fig-detrend
#| fig-cap: "Periodogram of a trending AR(1) series without detrending (left) and with detrending (right). The trend dominates the low frequencies until it is removed."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

set.seed(3)
y_trend = 0.05 * (1:300) + arima.sim(list(ar = 0.5), n = 300) + 2 * sin(2 * pi * (1:300) / 10)
sp_raw = spec.pgram(y_trend, detrend = FALSE, demean = TRUE, taper = 0, plot = FALSE)
sp_det = spec.pgram(y_trend, detrend = TRUE, taper = 0.1, plot = FALSE)

trend_pg = bind_rows(tibble(freq = sp_raw$freq, spec = sp_raw$spec, prep = "Not detrended"),
                     tibble(freq = sp_det$freq, spec = sp_det$spec, prep = "Detrended"))
trend_pg$prep = factor(trend_pg$prep, levels = c("Not detrended", "Detrended"))

ggplot(trend_pg, aes(freq, spec)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_obs) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 1 / 10, linetype = "dashed", colour = col_ref) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~prep, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = "Spectrum (log scale)", title = "The effect of detrending.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

In @fig-detrend the series also has a period-10 cycle (dashed line). Without detrending, the trend puts huge power at the lowest frequencies, which leaks into the neighbouring frequencies. After detrending, the low-frequency power drops and the cycle stands out more clearly.

## Spectral signatures of familiar models

```{r}
#| label: fig-signatures
#| fig-cap: "Theoretical spectral densities (unit innovation variance) of five processes."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

f_grid = seq(0.001, 0.5, length.out = 500)
sig_df = bind_rows(
  tibble(freq = f_grid, S = arma_spec(f_grid), process = "White noise"),
  tibble(freq = f_grid, S = arma_spec(f_grid, ma = 0.7), process = "MA(1), theta = 0.7"),
  tibble(freq = f_grid, S = arma_spec(f_grid, ar = 0.7), process = "AR(1), phi = 0.7"),
  tibble(freq = f_grid, S = arma_spec(f_grid, ar = -0.7), process = "AR(1), phi = -0.7"),
  tibble(freq = f_grid, S = arma_spec(f_grid, ar = c(1.5, -0.75)), process = "AR(2), complex roots")
)
sig_df$process = factor(sig_df$process, levels = unique(sig_df$process))

ggplot(sig_df, aes(freq, S)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_obs, linewidth = 0.8) +
  facet_wrap(~process, scales = "free_y", ncol = 3) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = "S(f)", title = "Spectral signatures.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

| Process              | Shape of $S(f)$                                 |
|----------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| White noise          | Flat at every frequency                         |
| MA(1)                | Monotone, sloping up or down                    |
| AR(1), $\phi > 0$    | Power concentrated at low frequencies ("red")   |
| AR(1), $\phi < 0$    | Power concentrated at high frequencies ("blue") |
| AR(2), complex roots | A peak at an interior frequency                 |
| Seasonal             | A narrow spike at $1/m$ and its harmonics       |

: Spectral signatures of familiar processes. {#tbl-signatures}

**Question: match the shapes (A) flat, (B) power near** $f = 0$, (C) power near $f = 1/2$, (D) a broad interior peak.

A is white noise, B is an AR(1) with positive $\phi$, C is an AR(1) with negative $\phi$, and D is an AR(2) with complex roots (@fig-signatures and @tbl-signatures).

### A cycle that is not seasonal

The AR(2) $y_t = 1.5y_{t-1} - 0.75y_{t-2} + \varepsilon_t$ has complex roots and a spectral peak at about $f \approx 0.08$, a period of about 12.4 observations:

```{r}
f_peak = f_grid[which.max(arma_spec(f_grid, ar = c(1.5, -0.75)))]
c(peak_frequency = f_peak, peak_period = 1 / f_peak)
```

**Question: would a periodogram peak near twelve months prove deterministic annual seasonality?**

No. An AR(2) with complex roots also gives a peak near 12 months, but its cycles vary in length from one cycle to the next and are not tied to the calendar. The width of the peak is the difference: a stochastic cycle gives a *broad* peak, while a deterministic seasonal pattern gives a *narrow* spike at $1/m$ (plus its harmonics).

## What differencing does to a spectrum

Filtering a series multiplies its spectrum by a fixed curve. For the first difference $(1-L)$ the curve is $|1 - e^{-2\pi i f}|^2 = 4\sin^2(\pi f)$, and for the seasonal difference $(1 - L^{12})$ it is $4\sin^2(12\pi f)$.

```{r}
#| label: fig-diff_gain
#| fig-cap: "Multipliers applied to the spectrum by the first difference (left) and the seasonal difference at lag 12 (right)."
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

gain_df = bind_rows(
  tibble(freq = f_grid, gain = 4 * sin(pi * f_grid)^2, filter = "First difference (1 - L)"),
  tibble(freq = f_grid, gain = 4 * sin(12 * pi * f_grid)^2, filter = "Seasonal difference (1 - L^12)")
)

ggplot(gain_df, aes(freq, gain)) +
  geom_line(colour = col_obs, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  facet_wrap(~filter, ncol = 2) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = "Multiplier", title = "Differencing as a filter.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The first difference multiplies the power at $f = 0$ by zero (it removes the level and strongly damps a trend), but it multiplies the power at $f = 1/2$ by four. The seasonal difference has zeros at $f = 0, 1/12, 2/12, \dots, 6/12$, so it removes the level and every seasonal harmonic (@fig-diff_gain).

```{r}
# Over-differencing white noise:
set.seed(5)
wn = rnorm(10000)
d_wn = diff(wn)

c(var_white_noise = var(wn),
  var_differenced = var(d_wn),
  acf_lag1_differenced = acf(d_wn, plot = FALSE)$acf[2])
```

**Question: why is unnecessary differencing harmful, not just unhelpful?**

Differencing is a filter, not just a trend remover: it removes low-frequency variation *and* amplifies high-frequency variation. If there is no trend, it removes a component that was not there and amplifies the fastest, least informative variation. Differencing white noise doubles the variance and creates a lag 1 autocorrelation of $-0.5$ (the output above), i.e. an MA(1) with $\theta = -1$, which is not invertible.

## The frequency domain versus the ACF

| Question                  | Time domain                   | Frequency domain               |
|----------------------|-------------------------|-------------------------|
| Is there dependence?      | ACF and PACF                  | The spectrum is not flat       |
| How long is the cycle?    | Awkward, from ACF peaks       | Directly, from a spectral peak |
| Is the cycle regular?     | Hard to judge                 | The width of the peak          |
| Several cycles at once?   | Very hard                     | Immediate                      |
| Which model should I fit? | ACF/PACF identification       | Not directly                   |
| Forecast the next value   | Directly, via a model         | Not directly                   |
| Non-stationary series     | Differencing, transformations | Requires stationarity          |

: When to use the time domain and when to use the frequency domain. {#tbl-domains}

The two domains contain the same information (the spectral density is the Fourier transform of the autocovariance function), but @tbl-domains shows that they make different questions easy. The frequency domain describes, but does not extrapolate, which is why ARIMA models are used for forecasting.

**Question: a series has cycles of roughly 7, 30 and 365 observations. Which representation makes these easier to see?**

The frequency domain. The three cycles appear as three separate peaks at $1/7$, $1/30$ and $1/365$, whereas the overlapping patterns in an ACF would be almost impossible to untangle.

## Integrated exercise

```{r}
#| label: fig-exercise_series
#| fig-cap: "The exercise series."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false

set.seed(314)
n = 360
y = 1.5 * sin(2 * pi * (1:n) / 30) + rnorm(n, 0, 0.8)

plot(ts(y), main = "Exercise series", ylab = expression(y[t]), xlab = "Time", col = col_obs)
```

**Task 1: predict, then read the periodogram.**

```{r}
pg = pgram(y)
pg |> slice_max(I, n = 5)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-exercise_pg
#| fig-cap: "Raw periodogram of the exercise series."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false

ggplot(pg, aes(freq, I)) +
  geom_segment(aes(xend = freq, yend = 0), colour = col_bar, linewidth = 0.4) +
  labs(x = "Frequency", y = expression(I(f)), title = "Raw periodogram.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The largest ordinate is at $f = 12/360 = 0.0333$, a period of 30 observations (@fig-exercise_pg). Since $360/30 = 12$, the cycle again lies exactly on a Fourier frequency. The next largest ordinates are about 60 times smaller. In the time plot (@fig-exercise_series) I could see that there is a cycle, but not its exact length.

**Task 2: smooth at two spans.**

```{r}
#| label: fig-exercise_smooth
#| fig-cap: "Smoothed spectra of the exercise series with spans = 9 (top) and spans = 15 (bottom). The dashed line marks f = 1/30."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 7

sp9  = spec.pgram(y, spans = 9,  taper = 0.1, detrend = TRUE, fast = FALSE, plot = FALSE)
sp15 = spec.pgram(y, spans = 15, taper = 0.1, detrend = TRUE, fast = FALSE, plot = FALSE)

par(mfrow = c(2, 1))
plot(sp9$freq,  sp9$spec,  type = "l", log = "y", col = col_obs,
     main = "Smoothed (spans = 9)",  xlab = "Frequency", ylab = "Spectral density")
abline(v = 1 / 30, lty = 2, col = col_ref)
plot(sp15$freq, sp15$spec, type = "l", log = "y", col = col_obs,
     main = "More smoothing (spans = 15)", xlab = "Frequency", ylab = "Spectral density")
abline(v = 1 / 30, lty = 2, col = col_ref)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```

The peak near $1/30$ survives the heavier smoothing (@fig-exercise_smooth). It becomes wider and a bit lower, but it is still far above the rest of the spectrum, which is roughly flat. Comparing two spans is the point: a real feature persists when the smoothing is increased a little, while a bump caused by noise tends to disappear.

**Task 3: formal test.**

```{r}
fisher_g_test(y)
```

Fisher's test rejects white noise with a tiny p-value, and the largest ordinate is at a period of 30. The test adds a formal statement that the largest ordinate is too large to be a chance maximum under white noise. The smoothed spectrum adds *where* the feature is and *how broad* it is.

**Final interpretation.** The spectrum has one dominant periodic component at about 0.033 cycles per observation, a cycle of about 30 observations. It survives moderate smoothing, so it is not a single noisy ordinate, and Fisher's test gives strong evidence against white noise. The rest of the spectrum is flat, which is consistent with white noise around the cycle. Since the noise appears to be white, I do not need to prewhiten the series before testing.

## Applying the routine to `AirPassengers`

To try the five steps on real data, I used the log of `AirPassengers`, detrended with a linear regression (the spectrum needs a stationary series).

```{r}
# Log, then remove a linear trend:
log_ap = as.numeric(log(AirPassengers))
t_ap = seq_along(log_ap)
ap_detrended = residuals(lm(log_ap ~ t_ap))

pgram(ap_detrended) |> slice_max(I, n = 6)
fisher_g_test(ap_detrended)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ap_spectrum
#| fig-cap: "Smoothed spectrum (spans = c(3, 3)) of detrended log(AirPassengers). The dotted lines mark the annual frequency 1/12 and its harmonics."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

sp_ap = spec.pgram(ap_detrended, spans = c(3, 3), taper = 0.1, plot = FALSE)

ggplot(tibble(freq = sp_ap$freq, spec = sp_ap$spec), aes(freq, spec)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = (1:6) / 12, linetype = "dotted", colour = col_ref) +
  geom_line(colour = col_obs) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Frequency (cycles per month)", y = "Spectrum (log scale)",
       title = "Spectrum of detrended log(AirPassengers).") +
  theme_minimal()
```

<!-- CHECK: the largest ordinates should be at periods 12, 6, 3 and 4 months. -->

The largest ordinate is at a period of 12 months, and the next largest are at 6, 3 and 4 months (@fig-ap_spectrum). Following Step 2, these are the harmonics of one annual pattern: the passenger seasonal pattern has a sharp summer peak, which a single sine wave cannot describe. I used `as.numeric()` on purpose: for a `ts` object with `frequency = 12`, `spec.pgram()` rescales the frequency axis to cycles per *year*, so the annual peak would appear at 1 instead of 1/12. There is also some power at the very lowest frequencies, which is the curvature in the trend that a straight line does not remove.

## Topic exploration: is the lynx cycle a real cycle? {#topic-exploration-is-the-lynx-cycle-a-real-cycle}

The tutorial warns that Fisher's test can reject white noise just because a series is autocorrelated, and that a cycle should be tested on the residuals of a fitted ARMA model. I wanted to see this on real data. The `lynx` data set (annual Canadian lynx trappings, 1821--1934) has a famous cycle of about ten years, but it is not tied to the calendar, so it might be a *stochastic* cycle (like the AR(2) above) rather than a deterministic one.

```{r}
log_lynx = log10(lynx)

# 1. Fisher's test on the series itself:
fisher_lynx = fisher_g_test(as.numeric(log_lynx))

# 2. Fit an AR(2) and test its residuals (prewhitening):
ar2_lynx = arima(log_lynx, order = c(2, 0, 0))
fisher_resid = fisher_g_test(as.numeric(residuals(ar2_lynx)))

# Peak of the fitted AR(2) spectrum:
phi_lynx = coef(ar2_lynx)[c("ar1", "ar2")]
f_lynx = f_grid[which.max(arma_spec(f_grid, ar = phi_lynx))]

kable(data.frame(
  Test = c("log10(lynx)", "AR(2) residuals"),
  g = c(fisher_lynx$g, fisher_resid$g),
  `p-value` = c(fisher_lynx$p.value, fisher_resid$p.value),
  `Period of largest ordinate (years)` = c(fisher_lynx$period, fisher_resid$period),
  check.names = FALSE
), digits = 4)

c(phi_lynx, AR2_peak_period = 1 / f_lynx)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-lynx
#| fig-cap: "Smoothed spectrum of log10(lynx) (pink) with the spectral density implied by the fitted AR(2) (purple, scaled by the innovation variance), and the smoothed spectrum of the AR(2) residuals (grey)."
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 4
#| echo: false
#| message: false
#| warning: false

sp_lynx  = spec.pgram(as.numeric(log_lynx), spans = c(3, 3), taper = 0.1, plot = FALSE)
sp_resid = spec.pgram(as.numeric(residuals(ar2_lynx)), spans = c(3, 3), taper = 0.1, plot = FALSE)
lynx_true = tibble(freq = f_grid, spec = arma_spec(f_grid, ar = phi_lynx, sigma2 = ar2_lynx$sigma2))

ggplot() +
  geom_line(data = tibble(freq = sp_lynx$freq, spec = sp_lynx$spec), aes(freq, spec), colour = col_obs) +
  geom_line(data = lynx_true, aes(freq, spec), colour = col_ref, linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(freq = sp_resid$freq, spec = sp_resid$spec), aes(freq, spec), colour = "grey50") +
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "Frequency (cycles per year)", y = "Spectrum (log scale)", title = "The lynx cycle.") +
  theme_minimal()
```

<!-- CHECK: expected p-value ~1e-20 for log10(lynx) at a period of 9.5 years, an AR(2) with phi about (1.38, -0.75), an AR(2) peak at about 10 years and a large p-value (about 0.5) for the residuals. -->

On the series itself, Fisher's test rejects white noise very strongly, with the largest ordinate at a period of about 9.5 years. But the fitted AR(2) has complex roots and a spectral peak at a period of about `r round(1 / f_lynx, 1)` years, and its spectral density follows the shape of the estimated spectrum (@fig-lynx). After removing the AR(2) dependence, the residual spectrum is roughly flat and Fisher's test no longer rejects (p = `r round(fisher_resid$p.value, 2)`).

So the ten-year lynx cycle is real, but it is well described as a *stochastic* cycle produced by AR(2) dynamics (which fits the predator-prey story: the population overshoots and then crashes), not as a fixed sinusoid. A deterministic model (for example a regression on a 10-year sine and cosine) would be the wrong model, because the cycle length varies from cycle to cycle. This also shows why the test on the raw series is misleading on its own: it rejects white noise, but that does not tell us *what kind* of periodic structure is present. The residual p-value is only approximate, because the AR(2) parameters were estimated from the same data.

## Reflection

The main thing I learned from this tutorial is that the periodogram is just a way of splitting the variance of a series by frequency, and that the raw periodogram is a very noisy estimate of the spectrum. I would previously have trusted a single tall peak. The harmonics were also new to me: I would have read the 6- and 4-month peaks of `AirPassengers` as separate cycles. The most difficult part was the scaling conventions (`pgram()` vs `spec.pgram()`, one-sided vs two-sided spectra, and the `frequency` argument of `ts()`), because the same series can give numbers that differ by constant factors. The lynx exploration connected the frequency domain back to the ARMA models from earlier in this section: a broad spectral peak can be produced by an AR(2), so finding a cycle in the spectrum does not by itself mean the cycle is deterministic.
